title: The Golden Age of AI Engineering — Alexander Embiricos & Romain Huet & Peter Steinberger, OpenAI
talk_summary: OpenAI engineers describe how agent work has shifted from juggling many terminal sessions to managing a long-running 'manager' agent that delegates to workers, enabled by server-side compaction, coordination, and event triggers. Peter Steinberger's segment gives the most concrete mechanism: a persistent manager that wakes on events, spawns workers, and returns a single reviewable artifact (PR + issue + diff) so the human only touches the outer loop.

takeaways.technique: Long-running manager agent that delegates to workers
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of the human scheduling many parallel sessions, one persistent manager agent receives events, decides fit against project goals, spawns worker agents, and returns one consolidated result for review.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Now, I mostly talk to a long-running manager, which delegates work to a team.

takeaways.what_they_do: Automation wakes the same manager agent when something happens (e.g. a new issue), so the loop runs without a human or a polling scheduler.
takeaways.evidence_quote: automation can wake the same manager when something happens

takeaways.what_they_do: Compaction is built into the API so long-running tasks keep a bounded context instead of dying or being restarted; they stopped optimizing around single sessions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: server-side compaction made long-running tasks reliable enough that I stopped optimizing around first sessions

takeaways.what_they_do: The manager returns one bundle — PR, original issue, proposed diff, maybe a video or a running build — so the human reviews once and leaves one note, then the loop continues and lands after checks pass.
takeaways.evidence_quote: When the manager needs me, it returns a PR, the original issue, the proposed diff

takeaways.technique: Separate test boxes for agent builds
takeaways.what_they_do: Agents run tests on a separate machine so the local host isn't saturated by parallel threads.
takeaways.evidence_quote: That's mostly fixed by using test boxes. So, agents can run tests on a separate machine.

takeaways.technique: Cheap-capable tier plus parallel attempts when speed allows
takeaways.what_they_do: They cite a cheaper model at half the cost for near-frontier intelligence, and argue high token speed lets an agent try 5-6 approaches in parallel and pick the best.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Brings GPT 5.5 level intelligence, but at half the cost.
